2611.31352.title: Spectroscopic identification of z>7 quasars with Roman Space Telescope

2611.31352.abstract: The Roman Wide Field Instrument grism will cover a large area over 1.0-1.93 micrometers, making it possible to search directly for Lyman-alpha breaks in quasars beyond redshift z = 7. We simulate quasars at z = 7.5-10 under HLWAS-like exposures with ESpRESSO, including PSF convolution, slitless dispersion, source and background Poisson noise, read noise, and Horne optimal extraction. Three Lyman-alpha equivalent-width (EW) prescriptions are used to bracket the uncertainty in line strength, and the extracted spectra are compared with M/L/T dwarfs and passive red galaxies using the spectral angle mapper. The Lyman-alpha-break completeness remains above 90% to J_AB approximately 23.7-24.1 and reaches 50% at J_AB approximately 24.3-24.7. Beyond J_AB approximately 25, the result depends strongly on the adopted EW distribution. In the fixed-redshift SAM test, the QSO recovery rate is TPR >= 0.982. None of the noisy brown-dwarf or red-galaxy test spectra is classified as a QSO. Because those test spectra are generated from the same finite parent libraries as the reference classes, this result measures the stability of the classification against noise within those libraries rather than an independently calibrated survey false-positive rate. At the faint end, the strongest astrophysical sensitivity in the present calculation is to the high-EW tail of the Lyman-alpha distribution.

2611.31355.abstract: AMORE6 is a strongly lensed ($\mu\simeq78$), intrinsically faint galaxy at $z=5.725$, previously proposed as a metal-free candidate from the absence of [OIII]$\lambda$5007 in NIRCam slitless spectroscopy. We present deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy of its brighter image, AMORE6-B. We detect HeII$\lambda\lambda$1640,4686, with HeII$\lambda$4686/H$\beta=0.080\pm0.015$ and EW(HeII$\lambda$4686)$=35\pm8$ Å, weak [OIII] ($R_3=0.25$) and CIV$\lambda\lambda$1548,51, and no other metal lines. H and He lines give negligible attenuation, $T_e\simeq2\times10^4$ K, and $Y=0.226^{+0.022}_{-0.024}$. The oxygen abundance, $12+\log(O/H)\simeq6.08^{+0.24}_{-0.80}$ (0.04-0.4% $Z_\odot$, depending on the calibration), is the lowest at its stellar mass, while C/O is near or above solar. Photoionization models of different ionizing sources favour metal-free stars with a top-heavy initial mass function (IMF), as in the self-polluted phase of simulated Population III (Pop III) galaxies, or a metal-poor population with a luminous hard X-ray source; ordinary metal-poor populations, very massive stars, and accretion-based sources are disfavoured. A full SED fit in the fiducial self-polluted scenario gives $1.3\times10^5\,M_\odot$ of Pop III stars formed within the last 4 Myr, which ionize mildly enriched gas and leak 86% of their ionizing photons. The HeII-to-Balmer ratio constrains the slope $x$ and characteristic mass $M_{ch}$ of the Pop III IMF jointly, to $90x-268\lesssim M_{ch}/M_\odot\lesssim172x-330$ ($3\sigma$; $M_{ch}\lesssim70\,M_\odot$ for a Salpeter slope), excluding the most top-heavy IMFs allowed by near-field constraints. X-ray binaries are a possible alternative, but require either a metal-poor population too young (1 Myr) to host compact objects and an X-ray luminosity far above that of metal-poor galaxies, or $2\times10^6\,M_\odot$ of older Pop III.2 stars whose metals were mostly expelled.

2611.31367.title: AGN feedback in the multiphase inner intracluster medium of a cosmological super-resolved galaxy cluster

figures.caption: Figure 1: Cluster selection.We show the mean cold gas mass ($T<10^{4.5}\,\mathrm{K}$) within the central 50 kpc of TNG-Cluster halos over $$$z=0$$$-$0.1$, as a function of halo mass at z=0. Halos are color-coded according to Lehle et al. (2024) as strong cool-core (SCC), weak cool-core (WCC), and non cool-core (NCC), based on their central cooling time at z=0. The red-outlined triangle corresponds to the Centaurus cluster (Olivares et al., 2019), and the black-circled marker shows the TNG-Cluster halo, whose ICs were selected for our super-resolved simulation (halo original ID 963). For visualization, halos with no cold gas are assigned a random value $<10^{7}\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$. Many halos contain a $>10^{7}\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ reservoir of cold gas, all of them being either SCC or WCC, with a weak correlation between cold gas mass and halo mass (Rohr et al., 2025, see also).

Figure 2: Numerical resolution. Radial profiles of gas mass resolution (left) and spatial resolution (right) within $R_{\text{500c}}$ of h963 from our super-resolved run (blue, all gas cells; light red, cold gas cells only) compared to TNG-Cluster (grey, all gas cells). Shaded regions indicate the 16th–84th percentile range. The dashed grey vertical line marks the boundary of the refinement region. The distance-dependent target mass of our ICM refinement scheme boosts both mass and spatial resolution in the BCG core. The smallest gas cells are dominated by the cold phase. The dips in the blue/grey curve (right panel) correspond to satellites or streams of dense, cold gas inflowing or outflowing from the galaxy.

Figure 3: Illustration of the super-Lagrangian scheme. The left panel shows the halo h963 in TNG-Cluster, while the right panel presents our super-resolved simulation of h963. We show a cross-section of the Voronoi tessellation of the gas, taken through a plane passing through the cluster center, color-coded by temperature. The black crosses denote the position of the central SMBH. Owing to the quasi-Lagrangian nature of Arepo and the fixed target gas cell mass ($\sim 10^{7}\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ in the TNG-Cluster halo versus $2.3\times 10^{4}\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ in the super-resolved halo), higher-density regions are naturally resolved by smaller cells. As a result, in the right plot, finer structures are resolved in the core: a higher number of small, cold structures emerges surrounded by layers of warmer gas, AGN-driven hot fronts, and gas turbulent motions with swirls and eddies are more sharply defined, all embedded within a more finely resolved hot halo.

Figure 4: Cold gas content. We show the cold gas mass fraction (left) and covering fraction (right, i.e., the surface fraction covered by cold gas) as a function of redshift. Solid curves show the quantities within the full super-resolved region (blue) or the core, $<50$ kpc, region (light red), while the grey dotted-dashed lines correspond to the fractions for the TNG-Cluster analog, computed within the same aperture as the full super-resolved region. The cold gas mass fractions are similar for both simulations and remain low ($<2\%$, blue and grey curves) until $z\sim 0.05$, when a merger sweeps out most of the remaining cold gas. However, the cold gas covering fraction is a factor 3-5 higher in the super-resolved halo, reflecting the larger spread of cold gas cloudlets. The fractions are higher in the core (up to 10 %), with the fluctuations corresponding to transient, more or less extended filamentary and/or disk-like structures in the central region.

Figure 5: The complex configurations and kinematics of the multiphase gas in h963. We show 200 by 200 kpc maps (+/- 20 kpc depth) at four different redshifts, with rows displaying gas pressure, density, inverse plasma beta (magnetic pressure over thermal gas pressure), entropy of the low-entropy gas (Cavagnolo et al., 2008; Cavagnolo et al., 2009, $K<50~\mathrm{keV\ cm^{2}}$;), and mass-weighted gas radial velocity of the low-entropy gas (with respect to the central SMBH, velocity color scale is capped to better highlight the inflowing and outflowing gas). The black crosses denote the position of the central most massive SMBH. The white arrows at $z=0.33$ and $z=0.08$ point to high-velocity outflowing gas in the path of AGN feedback outbursts. 2611.31367.abstract: The intracluster medium (ICM) of galaxy cluster cores is a multiphase environment regulated by active galactic nuclei (AGN) feedback. Extended cool gas nebulae with complex morphologies and kinematics are commonly observed in cool-core clusters, but their origin and interaction with AGN feedback remain poorly understood. We present a cosmological magnetohydrodynamical zoom-in simulation of a low-mass cool-core galaxy cluster ($M_{\mathrm{200c}}=2.3\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$), using initial conditions from TNG-Cluster and the IllustrisTNG galaxy formation model. Through super-Lagrangian refinement, we achieve a baryonic mass resolution of $2.3\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ and a spatial resolution of $\sim40\text{-}90$ pc in the cool ($10^{4}\,\mathrm{K}<T<10^{5.5}\,\mathrm{K}$) gas phase within the central $370$ ckpc, while retaining the full cosmological context. We investigate the properties and evolution of cool clouds and filaments and their interaction with AGN feedback at $z\leq0.35$. The cluster core hosts a rich population of dense, low-entropy filaments, including inflowing and outflowing structures and occasional rotationally supported disks. Comparing simulations with AGN kinetic feedback turned off and on, we find that AGN activity fragments and redistributes the cool gas and increases its covering fraction without destroying the cool gas reservoir. Individual outbursts drive transient increases in the velocities and velocity dispersions of both cool and hot gas, on short, $\lesssim 50$ Myr, timescales. We also identify low-entropy gas uplifted by AGN-driven outflows. While feedback globally heats the ICM and offsets cooling, it also creates conditions that may favor local thermal instabilities -- through shock compressions, mixing, turbulence, and uplift.

2611.31382.abstract: Quasar companions at high redshifts are usually gas-rich star-forming galaxies whose molecular gas masses ($M_{\mathrm{mol}}$) are estimated from [C II], dust emission or a single mid-$J$ CO line. We detect CO(5-4) and [C I](1-0) with ALMA in LAE-2, a Ly$\alpha$-associated companion of the $z=4.7$ quasar in BR1202-0725, and CO(5-4) at the location near LAE-1, the Ly$\alpha$ emitter between the quasar and the submillimeter galaxy (SMG). With the CO(2-1) flux from the literature, LAE-2 has an $L'_{\mathrm{CO(5-4)}}/L'_{\mathrm{CO(2-1)}}$ ratio of $0.22\pm0.04$, as in high-redshift main-sequence galaxies but four times lower than in the quasar host and the SMG. A non-LTE model places the CO(5-4) excitation temperature only 4 K above the cosmic microwave background (CMB), yet the same gas would show an even lower ratio against the $z=0$ CMB. The CMB-corrected $M_{\mathrm{mol}}$ from [C I], $\approx9\times10^{10} M_{\odot}$, agrees with the independent [C II] estimate, whereas CO(5-4) gives a four times lower mass if assumed thermalized at 40 K with the same CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor. Combining our 3 mm measurement with archival far-infrared photometry, we find cold ($\approx25$ K) dust and main-sequence star formation, with a gas-to-stellar mass ratio of $\approx4$ and a depletion time of $\approx0.7$ Gyr. Its star formation can supply the far-ultraviolet field that the [C I], [C II], and CO lines require. Quasar companions can thus retain massive, weakly excited molecular gas reservoirs that mid-$J$ CO surveys can miss.

2611.31385.abstract: Quasars powered by rapid accretion onto supermassive black holes (SMBHs) have been uncovered deep into the first gigayear of cosmic history. We present the discovery of EUCL J150452.291+625224.39 (J1504+6252), selected from Euclid Wide Survey imaging and spectroscopically confirmed as the first quasar at z > 8 through observations with Keck, HST, LBT, and JWST. J1504+6252 exhibits the defining spectral signatures of archetypal quasars at lower redshift, including a luminous blue power-law continuum and broad permitted emission lines, indicating a classical broad-line region. JWST/NIRSpec G395M spectroscopy yields a systemic redshift of z = 8.129 +/- 0.005, corresponding to 630 Myr after the Big Bang and shifting the quasar redshift frontier by about 39 Myr (6% of the age of the Universe at that epoch). From H-beta and Mg II, we measured intrinsic broad-line-region FWHM of 3160 +/- 270 and 3740 (+160/-170) km/s, respectively. A widely used single-epoch H-beta calibration gives a reference black hole mass of log10(MBH/Msun) = 8.56 +/- 0.43. Applying a range of calibrations to both Mg II and H-beta yields log10(MBH/Msun) = 8.33-8.89 and Eddington ratios of 0.12-0.44. Assembling a black hole of several hundred million solar masses within the first few hundred million years, despite its currently sub-Eddington accretion rate, requires either a massive seed or sustained, highly efficient early growth. The discovery of a mature, sub-Eddington quasar at z > 8 suggests that substantially more luminous quasars hosting similarly massive black holes may remain to be discovered. Conversely, previously known reionisation-era quasars may represent the rapidly accreting end of a broader population of already massive black holes spanning a wider range of accretion states.

2611.31387.abstract: We demonstrate that microphysical processes at the disk--halo interface, typically unresolved in circumgalactic medium (CGM) simulations, strongly affect the thermodynamic structure and observational signatures of an inflowing hot ($\sim10^6\,{\rm K}$) CGM. If the hot gas is pulled through the interface faster than it can cool, e.g.\ by turbulent mixing with the ISM or fountain flows, the hot CGM approaches an isentropic state. If instead the interface is regulated by radiative cooling on the hot gas cooling time, the hot CGM develops an outward-increasing entropy profile akin to a classic cooling flow. The two regimes differ by a factor of $\sim\!10$ in the predicted hot gas density above the disk near the rotation axis, and consequently by a factor of $\sim100$ in the predicted X-ray emission measure. We show that an isentropic CGM is produced in idealized CGM simulations that fail to resolve the pc-scale disk--halo interface, as numerical mixing drives artificially rapid cooling at the interface. A similar isentropic structure is found along the rotation axis in FIRE zoom-in simulations of $z\sim0$ Milky-Way-mass galaxies, where the cooling layer is likewise unresolved, raising the possibility that numerical mixing contributes to the isentropic structure. In contrast, an outward-increasing entropy profile forms in our idealized simulations when we replace the unresolved interface with an inner boundary that enforces a slow inflow. This outward-increasing entropy profile is likely also present in the Milky Way hot CGM, inferred from comparing density estimates at $\sim100\,{\rm kpc}$ with the entropy of the eROSITA bubbles.

2611.31415.abstract: Broad absorption line (BAL) quasars offer a powerful view into the structure, kinematics, and feedback mechanics of active galactic nuclei. In this study, we track the dramatic behavior of intrinsic CIV outflows of the quasar SDSS J142129.40+522752.0 at z = 3.228. We analyze 199 high-signal- to-noise optical spectra collected over a 12-year baseline via the Sloan Digital Sky Survey III/IV Reverberation Mapping and the SDSS-V Black Hole Mapper Reverberation Mapping programs. We quantify multi-year variability across two prominent absorption features: a primary high-velocity CIV BAL trough (Trough A) and a lower-velocity mini-BAL (Trough B). Both troughs exhibit rapid, significant variations in equivalent width and average depth, culminating in temporary disappearances during the 2022-2023 observing seasons before reappearing at their original velocities. We find that the behavior of the two troughs is highly correlated with both the g-band flux and each other, strongly indicating that the observed variability is driven by ionization state changes of the gas. The equivalent width of the mini-BAL Trough B is found to lag that of Trough A by ~4 days in the quasar rest frame, suggesting that the equilibrium timescales of the two absorbers are different and possibly indicative of different outflow densities or distances.

2611.31633.abstract: We report the detection of the forbidden pure rotational spectrum of H$_3^+$ in the Ring Nebula (NGC 6720), to our knowledge the first detection of H$_3^+$ in a planetary nebula. In JWST/MIRI spectra obtained toward the inner edge of the main ring, 0.1 pc in projection from the central star, the $(J,K) = (5,0)\to(4,3)$ line at 16.325 $\mu$m is detected at $32\sigma$, along with nine further unblended lines. The H$_3^+$ emission spatially follows the H$_2$ emission, whose rotational lines show warm (660 K) and hot (1700 K) components. A statistical-equilibrium model at these temperatures reproduces the subthermal H$_3^+$ line pattern, with much of the emission arising in the hot H$_2$. The emission requires an H$_2$ ionization rate of $\sim 3\times 10^{-12}\,{\rm s^{-1}}$ in the hot H$_2$ for an electron fraction of $2\times 10^{-4}$. The rate is $\sim 2\times 10^4$ times the cosmic-ray ionization rate in diffuse clouds. The extreme-ultraviolet and soft X-ray radiation (54-300 eV) of the 135 kK central star supplies this rate if the hot H$_2$ lies within an H-nucleus column density of (4-8)$\times 10^{19}\,{\rm cm^{-2}}$ of the ionization front of the dense globules. Static photoionization models, however, place the H$_2$ in gas too cold to excite the H$_3^+$ lines. The warm molecular gas and its H$_3^+$ thus suggest dynamical effects, most plausibly the advection of H$_2$ through a photoevaporation front into gas heated by the star. H$_3^+$ provides a new probe of the photoionization of molecular gas by very hot stars.

2611.31785.abstract: Cosmological simulations often account for unresolved density fluctuations using a sub-grid clumping factor when modeling chemical reactions. To validate this approach, we conduct hydrodynamical simulations of isothermal, supersonic turbulence and track the evolution of passive chemical species in first-, second-, and third-order reactions, exploring seven reaction rates across Mach numbers $M$ = 2-50 in three turbulence driving modes. We parametrize the saturation of clumping factors at $M \gtrsim 10$ due to intermittency (i.e., falling significantly below the log-normal prediction) with a one-parameter fitting formula. Furthermore, we find that the competition between turbulent mixing and the density-dependent reaction rates, governed by the Damköhler number (Da), suppresses the global reaction rate by a \textit{mixing efficiency} factor ($\xi$). For Da $\ll 1$, chemical species remain well mixed ($\xi\to 1$), and the reaction rates are boosted by a clumping factor. For Da $\gg 1$, reactants in dense gas are rapidly depleted before being redistributed by turbulence, causing $\xi$ to drop by a factor of a few to more than an order of magnitude. We quantify the effective mixing efficiency as a function of two dimensionless parameters, $M$ and Da, and provide a fitting formula that can be easily adopted in cosmological simulations to accurately follow unresolved chemical reactions.

2611.32173.abstract: The discovery of amino acids on asteroids, including samples returned from asteroid Bennu, and the detection of glycine on comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko support the hypothesis that glycine can form in extraterrestrial environments. Laboratory experiments show that glycine can form through both energetic and non-energetic processing of interstellar ice analogues. In the interstellar medium, glycine is exposed to various forms of energetic processing, including cosmic rays and the secondary electrons they generate, which have been shown to produce complex organic molecules, including peptides. This work investigates whether peptide-forming chemistry is a general consequence of energetic processing. Films of glycine and glycine-d3 were grown in two ultrahigh-vacuum chambers and irradiated with 1-2 keV electrons. The irradiated samples were subsequently characterised using infrared spectroscopy, temperature-programmed desorption, and vacuum-ultraviolet spectroscopy. Peptide formation through condensation reactions would produce water as a secondary product, and spectra obtained following irradiation of glycine-d3 showed evidence of D2O formation, supported by TPD measurements, which revealed H2O formation for glycine and H2O, HDO, and D2O for glycine-d3. VUV spectra of irradiated glycine showed the formation of decomposition products, including CO and CO2, as well as H2O. Following heating, a non-volatile residue remained on the surface. Electron irradiation of glycine produces reaction products similar to proton irradiation, suggesting that the resulting chemistry is not strongly dependent on the energy source. These findings support the possibility that larger organic molecules can form in a wide range of extraterrestrial environments. Such molecules may subsequently be incorporated into small bodies and delivered to planetary surfaces, potentially contributing to the emergence of life.

2611.32342.abstract: Detailed studies with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) have shown that dust is widespread even in UV-luminous galaxies at $z\gtrsim6.5$. Multi-band continuum observations are critical to fully characterize these early dust reservoirs. We present a homogeneous analysis of multi-band ALMA observations from the REBELS Large Program and seven follow-up programs, targeting thirteen massive galaxies at $6.5\lesssim z\lesssim7.7$ in at least two bands, including Band 8. Through optically thin modified blackbody fitting, we infer the dust masses, temperatures, and infrared luminosities of our targets. Their dust temperatures span $T_\mathrm{dust}\approx30-70\,\mathrm{K}$, and a stack reveals an average $T_\mathrm{dust}=49_{-8}^{+11}\,\mathrm{K}$. Three sources nominally qualify as ultra-luminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs; $L_\mathrm{IR}>10^{12}\,L_\odot$), with total star formation rates of $\mathrm{SFR}_\mathrm{UV+IR}\approx160-300\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, the highest of which is found in our most distant target, REBELS-18 at $z=7.67$. Their star formation is heavily obscured, with $\gtrsim90\%$ emerging in the infrared, compared to an already large average obscured fraction of $f_\mathrm{obs}=0.75\pm0.11$ for the stack. These SFRs are consistent with the reconstructed growth histories of some massive quiescent galaxies at $z\approx4-5$, suggesting that dusty yet UV-bright galaxies at $z\sim7$ are plausible progenitors of such systems. The sample moreover displays large dust-to-stellar mass ratios ($M_\mathrm{dust}/M_\star = 0.4_{-0.2}^{+0.3}\%$), best reproduced by models in which dust grows efficiently in the interstellar medium. 2611.32592.abstract: The infrared excess (IRX = L_IR / L_UV) of star-forming galaxies (SFGs) follows a tight scaling relation with star formation rate, gas-phase metallicity, and size up to z ~ 3, providing a key benchmark for galaxy formation models. We test whether TNG50 SFGs, post-processed with the radiative transfer code SKIRT, reproduce the universal IRX relation - linking IRX to metallicity, infrared luminosity, size, and inclination - and identify the origin of any offsets. We analyse 7280 TNG50-SFGs across 0 <= z <= 4, comparing their predicted IRX relations with observations and the EAGLE simulation. We test different dust-to-metal (DTM) ratios and dust compositions, recalibrate galaxy properties to observed scaling relations, and decompose the offsets into individual parameter contributions. TNG50-SFGs match the universal IRX relation closely at 0.5 <= z <= 1, but lie above it at z = 0 (+0.5 dex) and below it at z >= 2 (-0.25 dex). They follow a relation of the same functional form, with a shallower, metallicity-independent L_IR slope. At z ~ 0, TNG50-SFGs are ~1 dex fainter in L_IR than the local calibration sample, requiring extrapolation; at fixed stellar mass and L_IR, simulated and observed IRX agree within 0.04 dex. At z >= 2, TNG50-SFGs are less obscured than predicted, an offset largely removed by lowering their metallicities by ~0.2 dex. Varying the DTM ratio and dust type shifts the offset normalisation without resolving its redshift evolution: a redshift-dependent DTM ratio helps at high z, but not at z = 0. Resolving the low-z discrepancy requires both improved dust models and observational constraints on IR-faint galaxies.

2611.32613.abstract: We present the first results of the Zero Enrichment Rare Objects (ZERO) survey, a narrow-band photometric survey targeting metallicity-sensitive narrow bands using the Hyper Suprime-Cam on the Subaru Telescope. This paper outlines the scientific goals, survey strategy, current observational status, photometric calibration, and metallicity estimation. The current ZERO footprint comprises 21 pointings, covering approximately 35 deg$^2$ along the celestial equator in the NB395 band, reaching NB395 $\sim$ 24.5 mag (10$\sigma$) in one hour, significantly deeper than typical comparable narrow-band Ca H\&K surveys. The NB395 photometry is calibrated using corrected Gaia BP/RP spectra and the recalibrated SDSS Stripe 82 catalog, achieving a typical zero-point precision of $\sim$0.3 per cent and flat-field precision better than 1 per cent on spatial scales larger than 8$^\prime$. Under typical conditions (three repeats; total exposure time $\sim$1 hour), the photometric precision reaches $\sim$1.1 per cent at NB395 $\approx$ 12, $\sim$1.5 per cent at 20, and $\sim$10 per cent at 24. We estimate [Ca/H] using a Physics-constrained Stellar Locus Fitting Method. The resulting [Ca/H] precision is better than 0.18 dex for sources brighter than NB395 $\sim$ 20, spanning a wide metallicity range from metal-rich to the very metal-poor regime ($-3 \le$ [Ca/H]$\le +0.5$). We further show that NB395 traces [Ca/H] more directly than [Fe/H]. The final catalog contains one million sources with NB395 photometry, including 379,216 repeatedly observed and 61,845 with [Ca/H] estimates. These results provide a solid foundation for future ZERO survey, including photometric calibration, stellar parameter determination, and investigations of Galactic structure and chemical evolution.

2611.31327.abstract: Planets form in disks of gas and dust. One step of their formation is the gathering of dust grains into dense clumps, under their own gravity. This work tries to predict when these clumps appear and how far apart they are. The grains attract each other through a gravity of finite range. The gas slows them down, and its turbulence spreads them out. The grains also cannot go beyond maximum packing: this is volume filling. The dimensionless model depends on two numbers. The first one is the gravitational number $\chi$, which compares attraction with turbulent spreading. The second one is the mean volume fraction $\rho_b$, which measures the amount of grains. We solve the model with second-order finite volumes on an adaptive Cartesian mesh. We then treat each field as an image. An Otsu threshold and a watershed transform isolate the clumps. The code conserves mass to within $10^{-15}$ and converges at second order. Two designs of experiments give 192 simulations in total, with $2\le\chi\le40$ and $0.05\le\rho_b\le0.7$. Linear stability theory predicts the start of clump formation. The instability starts at time $t_{on}\simeq3.0/\sigma^*$, where $\sigma^*$ is the growth rate of the most amplified mode. The dominant wavelength equals the most amplified wavelength to within $10\%$. The area fraction of the clumps equals $\rho_b$. The clumps then go through slow coarsening. A sensitivity analysis attributes most of the variance to $\chi$. The adaptive mesh reduces the computational cost only a little, because the clumps fill the whole domain.

2611.31361.abstract: Dense stellar environments surrounding massive black holes (MBHs) provide a natural setting for dynamical interactions that can produce transient electromagnetic and gravitational-wave sources. In particular, the tidal field of an MBH can strongly perturb binaries undergoing close encounters with it, driving their internal orbits to extreme eccentricities. Here, we investigate the outcomes of such interactions for binaries composed of a stellar-mass black hole (BH) and a star. Using direct few-body scattering experiments with the code SpaceHub, we explore hyperbolic encounters between BH-star binaries and MBHs. We systematically quantify the probabilities of different dynamical outcomes as functions of the binary orbital parameters and MBH mass, with particular emphasis on a channel in which the tidally induced eccentricity triggers a micro-tidal disruption event ($\mu$TDE), as the star is disrupted by its BH companion, followed by accretion of the stellar debris onto the MBH. We derive fitting formulae for the $\mu$TDE cross section and for the time delay between the two resulting flares, finding that the latter can be a few months for an MBH of $10^6\,M_\odot$. These double transients offer a distinctive observational signature of $\mu$TDEs. We estimate event rates ranging from a few to $\sim 100\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ within a luminosity distance of $40\,{\rm Gpc}$.

2611.31364.abstract: Studying the implications of self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) on astrophysical objects often requires simulations. N-body simulations are a standard tool but face a few challenges. One is resolving the mean free path in gravothermally collapsing halos. This is necessary to obtain accurate results and is achieved in state-of-the-art simulations by increasing the number of resolution elements. I aim to formulate a numerical scheme that gives an enhanced spatial resolution compared to those methods and allows increasing the resolution without changing the number of resolution elements. The novel scheme that I present is formulated by discarding the classic approach of using kernel functions and computing interaction probabilities. Instead, pairs of particles always interact if their distance is below a specific threshold. Importantly, this distance threshold depends on their relative velocity and the size of the time step. This new formulation no longer requires some of the computations in state-of-the-art schemes and thus helps to increase the performance. Through a variety of test problems with known solutions, I study the accuracy of the new scheme and demonstrate its advantages over state-of-the-art SIDM formulations. Notably, the scheme reduced the computational costs, making the SIDM computations typically much cheaper than gravity. As a consequence, a typical SIDM simulation of isotropic scattering requires only a few percent of its total computational cost for the self-interactions. In conclusion, the new scheme presents an improvement over previous schemes and helps to address current challenges. Besides the enhanced performance, it allows us to achieve a higher accuracy when simulating gravothermally collapsing SIDM halos.

2611.31386.abstract: Sub-kiloparsec X-ray structures in active galactic nuclei (AGN), including outflows, jets, and dual AGN, provide key insights into their evolution and influence on host galaxies. In the local universe, Chandra X-ray Observatory's state-of-the-art $0.5''$ angular resolution has resolved these structures, but at $z > 0.1$, milliarcsecond resolution is required to spatially resolve sub-kpc scales. We leverage the spatial amplification by strong gravitational lensing to investigate the X-ray structure of J1721+8842, a $z=2.38$ quasar lensed into six images. To reconstruct the optical emission position, we model the lensing mass distribution using the six quasar images, five detected by Gaia Data Release 3 (A-E) and one by HST (F). Our model reproduces the five Gaia image positions to milliarcsecond precision. To locate the X-ray emission relative to the optical, we combine ray-trace simulations of archival Chandra observations with the lens model image position predictions using a double maximum-likelihood analysis. We constrain the X-ray centroid within a $0.017''\times0.004''\ (139\times30\ \mathrm{pc})$ ellipse centered $0.005''\ (44\ \mathrm{pc})$ away from the optical source position. Source-plane reconstructions of the soft-X-ray and hard-X-ray to optical sources demonstrate these emission regions are cospatial, allowing the optical source at $1\sigma$ confidence. These results indicate no evidence for kpc-scale X-ray jets, outflows, or dual AGN with projected separations exceeding $140\ \mathrm{pc}$. This method improves Chandra's effective angular resolution by a factor of 30 at cosmological distances, enabling studies of sub-kpc AGN X-ray structure at cosmic noon.

2611.31418.abstract: We reassess the abundance ratio between elements at the third rapid neutron-capture process (r-process) peak (Os, Ir, Pt) and the lanthanide element Eu. We show that some weak optical lines of Os I, Ir I, and Pt I yield abundances inconsistent with stronger ultraviolet (UV) and optical lines and provide recommendations for their limited use alongside more reliable lines. We perform a meta-analysis of Os, Ir, and Pt abundances from 35 studies of 77 r-process-enhanced metal-poor stars spanning -3.43 < [Fe/H] < -1.27 and +0.22 < [Eu/Fe] < +2.45. The mean third-peak to lanthanide abundance ratios are $\log\varepsilon$(Os/Eu) = 0.86 $\pm$ 0.02, $\log\varepsilon$(Ir/Eu) = 0.88 $\pm$ 0.03, and $\log\varepsilon$(Pt/Eu) = 1.12 $\pm$ 0.04, which agree with the inferred Solar System r-process ratios to within 0.05 dex. These abundance ratios vary by less than 0.50 dex (a factor of 3.2), 0.56 dex (a factor of 3.6), and 0.45 dex (a factor of 2.8), respectively, in 90 percent of the r-process events that enriched metal-poor stars in existing samples. We use a representative r-process model to show that the small range of stellar abundance ratios favor models with a substantial contribution from neutron-rich material, with electron fractions, $Y_e$, < 0.2. We conclude that the third-peak to lanthanide abundance ratios are robust in existing r-process-enhanced star samples. In two stars with [Eu/Fe] < 0, the upper limits derived from non-detection of Pt indicate that the third-peak elements are deficient relative to lanthanides, and we conclude that this may be a signature of the limited r-process.

2611.31943.abstract: Searches for radio technosignatures have concentrated on narrowband signals. We present a complementary search for excess broadband 2-4 GHz emission from 210,191 Gaia DR3 main-sequence stars within 100 pc in all epochs of the VLA Sky Survey (VLASS; 2017-2026). Cross-matching with the Epoch-1 catalog yields 51 high-reliability positional associations (versus 1.5 expected by chance). All but one are known natural emitters that, where measurable, move with their stars; the remaining source, near LSPM J1943+5337, is not at the star. Because stellar flares can mimic transmitters in continuum flux, a detection counts as a possible transmitter at any luminosity only at the 32,985 apparently single AFGK stars outside known radio-emitter classes, and at M dwarfs and AFGK multiples only above $10^{10}$ W Hz$^{-1}$. Forced photometry of 208,232 stars in all epochs finds 1 steady-test detection and 3 stars detected in at least one epoch among the eligible stars, against 1.3 and 1.9 expected by chance. The median per-star limit on steady emission is $L_u<4.0\times10^{8}$ W Hz$^{-1}$. Without background subtraction, fewer than $1.5\times10^{-4}$ of eligible AFGK stars host a steady transmitter above $10^9$ W Hz$^{-1}$, and fewer than $2.3\times10^{-5}$ of all stars outside the known-emitter classes host one above $\sim1.1\times10^{10}$ W Hz$^{-1}$; counting every M-dwarf detection as a possible transmitter, fewer than $5.5\times10^{-4}$ of M dwarfs host one above $10^9$ W Hz$^{-1}$. Stacks detect population-averaged emission from M dwarfs, concentrated in those with activity evidence. Continuum surveys thus constrain broadband, modulated, or rapidly drifting signals that narrowband pipelines do not search for.

2611.32656.abstract: We present a study of the binary fraction and mass-ratio distribution for near 200,000 FGK dwarf stars within 1 kpc, utilizing the Stellar Locus Outlier (SLOT) method applied to synthetic Gaia XP photometry and stellar parameters from LAMOST DR9. By modeling the asymmetric color residuals relative to a metallicity-dependent single-star locus, we measure the binary fraction $f_b$ and constrain the power-law slope $\gamma_{\rm large\,q}$ of the mass-ratio distribution at high mass ratio $q$. Higher metallicity is associated with a steeper (more negative) $\gamma_{{\rm large}q}$, indicating a larger proportion of low-mass-ratio systems. For $\alpha$-elements, [Mg/H] and [Si/H] are anticorrelated with $f_b$ in thin-disk-dominated subsamples; conversely, [Ca/H] shows a positive correlation with $f_b$ in thin-disk-dominated subsamples. No correlation is found between $f_b$ and $\alpha$-element abundances in thick-disk-dominated subsamples. The binary fraction increases modestly toward older ages in the thin-disk population, a trend that likely reflects underlying correlations with chemistry. Our results shed light on how chemical composition and dynamical processes shape the binary properties of solar-type stars.

2611.32808.abstract:
Context. The Magellanic Clouds System (MCS), comprising the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds (LMC and SMC) and the Magellanic Bridge (MB), offers a nearby laboratory for studying massive stars. Existing catalogs are limited by extinction, crowding, and incomplete cross-validation with the literature.
Aims. We identify candidate stars with initial masses of roughly 8 solar masses or more, including O- and early-B-type stars, supergiants, luminous blue variables, and Wolf-Rayet stars. We aim to improve completeness in reddened and crowded regions and recover sources missed by large surveys.
Methods. We combine Gaia DR3 astrometry and photometry with SIMBAD, HST, and complementary optical and infrared surveys. We select candidates using color-magnitude and color-color diagrams, extinction tracks, Gaia astrometry and variability, and spectral classifications. We check for duplicates and multiple systems, include literature and HST-resolved sources without reliable Gaia counterparts, especially in 30 Dor, and derive synthetic Gaia photometry where Gaia measurements are incomplete.
Results. ALS IV contains 51 954 massive star candidates: 36 506 in the LMC, 15 264 in the SMC, and 184 in the MB. It provides homogeneous identifiers and coordinates, multiwavelength photometry, astrometry, variability diagnostics, and spectral classifications where available. Complementary photometry and HST observations recover reddened and crowded sources missed by Gaia-based selections. The sample traces the main massive-star populations and prominent star-forming regions across the MCS.
Conclusions. ALS IV provides the most comprehensive census of massive star candidates in the MCS and serves as a reference for massive-star studies and future surveys and Gaia releases.

2611.32856.abstract: DG Tau is one of the best-studied young stellar objects in transition from a Class I protostar to a T Tauri star. It is no longer embedded in a dense molecular cloud, but still reveals features that are commonly seen in protostars at earlier evolutionary stages. DG Tau hosts a protoplanetary disk and two energetic jets that can be studied down to the immediate environment of the star and disk at optical, infrared, and X-ray wavelengths. We use the Medium Resolution Spectrometer of MIRI on the James Webb Space Telescope. DG Tau's mid-infrared spectrum consists of a very bright continuum with various silicate features, and lines of CO, H$_2$O, OH, H I, H$_2$, Ne$^{+}$, Ne$^{2+}$, Ar$^{+}$, Fe$^{+}$, and Ni$^{+}$. We find substantial grain growth to at least 2 $\mu$m at an early evolutionary stage. Lines of H$_2$O and CO are formed at extremely high temperatures (600-2000 K). The ratio of warm to hot water is the lowest among previous observations of disks with JWST. This and a very strong continuum point toward the relevance of the strong accretion of DG Tau and consequently strong stellar UV irradiation. The pair of jets reveals a rich spectrum of emission lines from ions, in particular producing forbidden lines of [Ne II], [Ne III], [Ar II], [Fe II], and [Ni II]. The forward jet shows a collimated structure as found previously, while the hitherto poorly described, receding jet is more widely dispersed on scales of several arcsec, showing a layered structure with the fastest components being the most collimated. The ionization of the jet gas cannot be reconciled with high-energy radiation from the star itself. Instead, we propose a unified nonequilibrium ionization shock model in which the previously studied X-ray jet plasma continuously cools, recombining ions until, at temperatures around $10^4$ K and below, metals at low ionization stages emit the observed ion lines.

2611.32906.abstract: An oscillating axion dark matter (DM) background can enhance the conversion of another relativistic axion into photons when traversing a magnetic field. The DM background rotates photon polarization relative the magnetic orientation, which compensates the photon's and the propagating axion's dispersion relation mismatch. We relate this mechanism to Axion Magnetic Resonance (AMR) and apply it to stellar axions in the starburst galaxy M82. We analyze its enhancement to the resulting X-ray signals while accounting for the finite magnetic domain size, dark matter coherence length, DM density morphology, plasma profiles, and the detector response. We derive strong constraints using existing X-ray data from NuSTAR. We show that this resonant conversion can lead to $\mathcal O(10^2)$ enhancement in the photon-axion conversion probability, improving the upper limits on axion's photon coupling over part of the mass range where ordinary conversion is suppressed. We also show that this type of resonance predicts distinctive features in the hard X-ray spectrum, which is moderately favored by the data over the background only model, yet it is currently still consistent with statistical fluctuations.

2611.33002.abstract: The properties of the eclipsing binaries SMC004701.39-732645.8, SMC005609.41-722809.2 and PW Pup are examined using archival photometric and spectroscopic observations. These systems have orbital periods of hundreds of days, and contain highly evolved components with temperature differences of at least 1000 - 2000K. The SMC systems are among the brightest eclipsing binaries in that galaxy at visible wavelengths, and show excess thermal emission that appears to be typical for luminous K and M giants in that galaxy. A preliminary mass function for SMC004701 suggests a minimum mass for the secondary of 3.8 +/- 0.8 Msolar, whereas the PW Pup mass function indicates a minimum mass for the secondary of 3.2 +/- 0.3 Msolar. Light curve elements are examined for a range of mass ratios using observations at visible and mid-infrared (MIR) wavelengths. The results suggest that SMC004701 may prove to be a double line spectroscopic binary at visible wavelengths. However, with the possible exception of emission from a circumstellar disk, infrared observations will likely be required to detect light from the secondary in the other two systems. All three systems have likely experienced mass transfer, and had components with initial masses that correspond to B spectral types on the main sequence. The light associated with the secondary likely originates from a shell or disk that obscures a hotter central star.

2611.33142.abstract: We present strong-lensing models for the 57 galaxy clusters observed in Cycle 4 out of the 60 targeted by the JWST Vast Exploration for Nascent, Unexplored Sources (VENUS) program. Models for the remaining three clusters will be incorporated after their observations. The dataset comprises 5013 individual images, corresponding to 1733 multiply-imaged systems, of which 912 have spectroscopic redshift measurements and 227 are newly identified. Using this new wealth of observations, we construct parametric lens models with our $\mathtt{AstroLensPy}$ software, reproducing the observed image positions with an average image-plane precision $\Delta_{\rm RMS}$ of $0.54''$. With a total imaging area of $576$ arcmin$^2$, VENUS offers the largest homogeneous set of cluster strong-lensing models to date. The clusters yield a combined area of $191$ arcmin$^{2}$ magnified by $|\mu|\geq3$ for a source $z_s=10$, for example, establishing the VENUS fields as a premier survey for high-redshift studies. Among our sample, the clusters MACS J0717.5+3745, RXC J0600.1-2007 and PLCK G287.0+32.9 display the largest Einstein radii ($\geq 60''$) and magnified areas ($\mathcal{A}_{z_s=10}^{|\mu|\geq3} \geq 9$ arcmin$^2$) for a source $z_s=10$, and therefore constitute the most potent gravitational telescopes known to date. Finally, leveraging the statistical power of the sample, we derive scaling relations between various lensing observables (Einstein radius, magnified area, projected mass) and the SZ/X-ray-inferred cluster mass, $M_{500,c}$.
